A1.justification: Both PDFs describe COMBO and retain matching core methods and experiments. All 23 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original TDW-Game and TDW-Cook experiments, generated-video evaluations, component ablations, and planning-budget and agent-count comparisons.

after.justification: v2 reports retained and revised TDW experiments, plus original COMBO results on 2D-FetchQ, component-level analyses, and a five-trial human–robot experiment.

M1.justification: The proposed COMBO procedure retains two-stage compositional diffusion training, agent-dependent loss scaling, state inpainting, three VLM planning modules, and the same tree-search algorithm. Explicit initial-frame conditioning clarifies the existing state-conditioned procedure. Appendix C.2 introduces a supervised comparison model without replacing the main COMBO method.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained TDW tasks, v2 adds visual 2D-FetchQ cooperation with replayed human trajectories and a physical human–XArm puzzle task using collected real-world training data. It also extends TDW-Game transfer evaluation to two agents. These substantially broaden task requirements and interaction environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons against BC-single, BC-GAIL, and Co-GAIL on 2D-FetchQ, plus a CLIP/BERT-based supervised model against the three VLM planning modules in Table 7. Existing TDW comparators and AVDC remain; Oracle Cooperator is renamed Shared Belief Cooperator, rather than removed.

E3.justification: v1 specifies a 60-step maximum and 10 episodes for the main TDW evaluation; v2 Table 1 reports success over a 30-step horizon and 20 episodes. New protocols include 60-episode human-trajectory replay, five physical trials, and component prediction-accuracy evaluation. Some v2 successful-episode averages exceed 30 steps, leaving their relationship to the stated horizon unclear.

E4.justification: v2 adds intent-tracker adaptation cases and prediction-error analysis, supervised-versus-VLM component comparisons, and a classification of world-model failures with visual examples in Appendix C. Agent-count generalization also extends to two agents. The existing loss-scaling and search-budget analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based variability, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Changed evaluation-episode counts and the new physical-trial count describe sample sizes, without introducing a different statistical uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main-table values change under revised reported settings: COMBO with TDW-Cook Cooperator 1 changes from 1.0 success/21.3 steps to 0.90/22.8, which is not a same-setting performance comparison. New results include 81.3% on 2D-FetchQ versus Co-GAIL's 53.3%, 100%/10.5 steps for two-agent TDW-Game, component accuracies in Table 7, and 4/5 physical successes with 8.4 average successful-trial steps. v1 Tables 2–3 retain their values as v2 Tables 3–4.

T1.justification: The DEC-POMDP formulation, score composition, diffusion losses, and sampling relationships retain their substance. New preliminary subsections reorganize and explain the existing diffusion mathematics, while explicit initial-frame conditioning clarifies notation. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the empirical scope from two custom benchmarks to evaluation on three benchmarks. The central claims about compositional world modeling, cooperative tree-search planning, and generalization across agent counts remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds explanations of intent adaptation through observation history, attributes VLM advantages to pretrained knowledge and multimodal integration, and proposes causes of generation failures involving guidance conflicts and action misunderstanding. It also discusses limits from restricted cooperator diversity and hidden physical variables. Appendix B adds possible alternatives when reachability information is unavailable; the existing slow-inference limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents 4,000 training environments, 40,000 intent-tracker rollouts, 138,000 evaluator examples, shared submodule models, and one-epoch LoRA fine-tuning with batch size, GPUs, and runtime. Appendix C.2 supplies the supervised comparator's architecture and training details, and Appendix D describes real-world fine-tuning. Existing diffusion-model sizes and budgets are retained. The project-video access link also changes.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 sharpens the comparison with VLP and newly discusses RoboDreamer's compositional robot planning. New citations support Co-GAIL evaluation, implementation details, and proposed extensions, while generic references such as Genie and NOPA disappear. These refine the existing multi-agent research positioning without replacing it.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the explanation: Problem Statement becomes part of expanded Preliminaries, Section 4 is rewritten around current-state and future-frame conditioning, and task and implementation descriptions move into separate appendices. The original appendix is reorganized into task and implementation sections alongside new analysis and real-world sections. Introduction wording, terminology, authorship, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, clarifies state and prediction labels in Figures 2 and 4, and adds Figures 8–13 for the new environment, intent tracking, failures, and physical experiments. It adds Tables 2, 7, and 8, combines success/steps within Table 1 cells, and expands the agent-count table. The conference template also changes typography, margins, headers, and figure placement throughout.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to two custom simulated tasks and left planning-module training substantially underspecified. v2 addresses these weaknesses through an additional cooperation benchmark, a physical pilot, component comparisons, intent and failure analyses, and concrete fine-tuning documentation. These materially improve empirical support and reproducibility. The physical study remains preliminary at five trials, and the stated 30-step horizon is difficult to reconcile with some reported averages, but these reporting limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.
